options.name: --finding
options.description:
Export only this finding (repeat for several; md/csv only -- html, pdf and acr
always write the whole report; not supported at all with --app, which always
writes the whole combined report). Ids are in each exported ticket's Provenance
section and the CSV's FindingId column; a given id that doesn't match anything
prints the ids actually in this run. Without --finding, every finding in the run
is exported
The finding to mark (with --status/--reason) or unmark (with --clear). With no
--finding at all, lists every finding this run currently has a mark for, plus any
mark that no longer matches a finding in this run ("stale")

options.name: --no-screenshots
options.description:
Leave screenshots out of the export (md: no images/ folder; html/pdf: nothing
embedded; csv and acr are unaffected, neither includes them). No privacy warning
here: a test device is assumed, the same as everywhere else Swipewalk captures a
screenshot

options.name: --triage
options.description:
Read triage marks from this file instead of the run's own triage.json. Every
format carries them: the CSV gets TriageStatus/TriageReason/TriageBy/TriageDate
columns, a Markdown ticket gets its own "## Triage" section, the HTML report shows
the same "Triaged by your team" group the report page does, and acr excludes a
finding marked false positive from its counts (disclosed in the row's remark) and
notes a won't-fix/accepted-risk mark next to the finding it still counts
Read and write marks in this file instead of the run's own triage.json -- e.g. a
project file committed alongside your app and shared across many runs of the same
app, rather than one run's own folder
A mark is never written into results.json (it stays a separate file, next to it); the run's report.html is
re-rendered immediately so it reflects the change without a rescan. A finding never reads as "fixed" or
"passed" because it was triaged -- it is still reported, just marked with who decided what and why.
Diagnostic log: every command also writes a short log on this computer (macOS ~/Library/Logs/Swipewalk,
Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Swipewalk\Logs, Linux ~/.local/state/swipewalk/logs or $XDG_STATE_HOME/swipewalk/logs):
versions, what ran, pre-flight results and errors, not the text on the screens you scan, with serial numbers,
device names, team IDs, your user name and home folder removed by pattern. Files more than a week old are
deleted, and older files are removed to keep the folder near 10 MB (checked when Swipewalk starts and once a day).
Set SWIPEWALK_LOG=debug in the terminal to also record the tool commands Swipewalk runs (adb, xcrun, xcodebuild...), with their arguments, exit codes and times.
Set SWIPEWALK_LOG_DIR to a full path to keep the log in another folder.
Nothing is ever sent; `swipewalk diagnostics` makes the file to attach to a bug report.
scan checks the screen currently shown (bringing the app forward, or starting it, first if needed).
record watches while you use the app; nothing is captured until you scan a screen (Enter, or --auto to
scan every new screen automatically). q finishes and writes the report. Exits with 2 if the recording
ended early (an error or a cancellation), and the report says so; screens after that point were not
scanned -- `record --continue <run>` resumes it later, appending screens to the same run rather than
starting a new one; the report then says it was recorded across more than one session, with each one's
times. If Swipewalk itself is closed or crashes mid-recording, there's no exit code to report that by --
but `swipewalk history` and `record --continue` notice the process is gone the next time you run them,
and list it as ended early, so it can be continued. run does what swipewalk.json describes and
exits with 3 when failOn is "wcag-issues" and issues were found. Output: results.json and report.html.
Automated checks find only some issues; manual testing is still required.

options.name: --source
options.description:
Path to the app's own project folder (.NET MAUI, native Android, native iOS,
React Native or Flutter), read locally to add a likely source line to findings
that don't already have one from the scan (see --source under Scan options
above). Useful when a run was scanned without the source available and the
source has since been found -- this only affects what's exported now, it never
rewrites the run's own results.json; not supported with --app

options.name: --app-name
options.description:
acr only: product name for the report (default: the scanned app's package/bundle
id, or "Scanned app" if that's not known either)

options.name: --author-email
options.description:
acr only: contact email for the report's required "author" field (default: an
obvious placeholder, noted in the draft as needing to be filled in before sharing
it -- never auto-filled from your local identity)

options.name: --author-name
options.description: acr only: contact name alongside --author-email (optional in the OpenACR format)

options.name: --app
options.description:
Instead of <run>: combine specific saved runs of this app id (Android package,
iOS bundle id) into one report, across the run history rather than one run.
Requires --app-version and --run; see: swipewalk history for the ids and versions
recorded. This report covers only the screens in the scans you give it --
Swipewalk can't tell which screens your app has, so make sure they cover what you
need

options.name: --app-version
options.description:
With --app: which recorded app version to combine runs of (exactly as shown by
swipewalk history; "version not recorded" selects runs with no recorded version).
You choose the version -- nothing is decided for you
The app version this decision was made against; optional, purely informational

options.name: --run
options.description:
With --app/--app-version: combine this run (repeat for several). Required --
nothing is included by default; without it, this lists the version's saved runs
with a one-line summary of each so you can choose. An id that isn't actually a
run of the given app/version is reported and skipped, never silently guessed at

options.name: --use
options.description:
With --app: if the given --run runs captured the SAME screen more than once,
says which run's capture to use for it (repeat for several such screens). Without
it, on an interactive terminal you're asked; otherwise the run fails and lists
every screen that still needs a choice, with its options

options.name: --history
options.description:
With --app: history folder to read from (default: the user's Swipewalk/runs folder)
Triage options (swipewalk triage):

options.name: --status
options.description:
What the team decided: false-positive (this isn't really an issue), wont-fix (a
real issue, not being fixed for now) or accepted-risk (a real issue the team is
knowingly leaving in place). For wont-fix and accepted-risk, everywhere the mark
is shown also states this never means the issue meets WCAG or any other standard.
Required together with --reason

options.name: --reason
options.description: Why (required together with --status; a triage mark is refused without one)

options.name: --by
options.description: Who made this decision, as free text (a name, a username, an email); optional

options.name: --clear
options.description:
Remove the current mark from --finding (its history is kept, not deleted -- see
the report's "stale" note if nothing else names this finding any more)

options.name: --harness-bundle-prefix

options.name: --install
options.description:
Install an already-built app first: Android .apk or App Bundle .aab; iOS Simulator
.app (or .zip); iOS device .ipa signed for the device. The app is never rebuilt or
re-signed. An .aab is installed via Google's bundletool (usually found on PATH, or

set of .apks for the connected device, then installs them, signed with the standard
Android debug key (~/.android/debug.keystore, created by Swipewalk with keytool if
it doesn't already exist) unless --keystore is given -- a debug-signed build
differs from your store build, for scanning only. Installing over an app already installed
with a different key fails; uninstall it first, or pass the matching --keystore

options.name: --bundletool
options.description:

usually found automatically when not given

options.name: --keystore
options.description:

debug key. Needs --keystore-alias, and the SWIPEWALK_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD environment
variable (SWIPEWALK_KEY_PASSWORD too if the key's own password differs -- rare for
a PKCS12 keystore, the default format since Java 8u60, which doesn't reliably
support a key password different from the keystore's own) -- a keystore password
is never taken on the command line or put in swipewalk.json

options.name: --keystore-alias
options.description: Android: key alias inside --keystore; required together with it

options.name: --package

options.name: --skip-checks
options.description: Skip the pre-flight checks that run before scan and record

options.name: --team
options.description:
iOS physical devices (also session --platform ios): Apple developer team that signs the scanning harness (found
automatically when the keychain has just one; a given team is remembered for next
time by `scan` run from a terminal, not by `record`, `session`, `swipewalk run`,
or a run whose input is redirected (scripts, CI))

options.name: --harness
options.description:
iOS: path to a harness project, for Swipewalk's maintainers (the harness that ships with
Swipewalk is used by default)

options.name: --android-harness
options.description:
Android: path to a harness project folder, for Swipewalk's maintainers (the prebuilt
harness that ships with Swipewalk is used by default; a missing or unbuildable harness
only skips Google's Accessibility Test Framework checks, never the scan -- see the
report/results.json for why)

options.name: --screen
options.description: Name for the scanned screen in the report (default: "Screen 1")

options.name: --out
options.description: Output directory (default: ./swipewalk-report); runs are also saved to the history

History folder to save to (scan, record and run; default: the user's Swipewalk/runs
folder). Given explicitly, runs re-scanned with --from are saved too

options.name: --from
options.description: Re-scan a saved capture directory instead of a live device

options.name: --carry-triage
options.description:
scan/record: after the run is saved, carry the triage marks of the previous run of the same app
and platform into it, the same way the desktop app does after every scan or recording: a mark is
carried only when exactly one finding on a matching screen matches it, never when more
than one could, and each carried mark says which run it came from. Off by default, so
existing output stays the same. Not with --no-history, --from or --continue

options.name: --triage
options.description:
scan/record: seed this run with an existing triage file's marks (see
`swipewalk triage`) before capturing anything, so its report shows them from the
start -- for a project file a team commits alongside their app (e.g.
swipewalk-triage.json). Without this, each run has its own triage.json in its
folder (the default `swipewalk triage <run>` writes to), started empty. compare and
export also accept --triage to read marks from elsewhere instead of the run's own
triage.json

options.name: --framework
options.description:
App framework for fix examples and the report header: maui, androidviews,
jetpackcompose, uikit, swiftui, flutter, reactnative or hybridweb. Detected
automatically when possible (Android: from its own class names; iOS: MAUI on the
Simulator or an iPhone installed with --install, a WebView filling the screen on
either platform; iOS never detects UIKit/SwiftUI, and detects Flutter/React
Native only from the app bundle) -- pass this to override detection, or to name
the framework yourself when it can't be detected (see docs/limitations.md
"framework-detection-partial")

options.name: --source
options.description:
scan/record/export: path to the app's own project folder, read locally to point
each finding at a likely source line (e.g. "Source (exact match):
Views/LoginPage.xaml:42" in the report and exported tickets; the label differs by
confidence, see the user guide). 0.4: .NET MAUI, native Android Views/Jetpack
Compose, native iOS (storyboards/XIBs, UIKit, SwiftUI), React Native and Flutter.
Which mapper runs is picked from each screen's own detected framework: MAUI (either
platform) uses the MAUI mapper; an Android screen detected as Views/Compose or not
detected at all uses the Android mapper; an iOS screen detected as UIKit/SwiftUI or
not detected at all uses the native iOS mapper; a React Native or Flutter screen,
on either platform, always uses its own mapper; a hybrid-web screen matches none of
them (a physical iPhone needs --install or --framework maui for MAUI detection, or
its findings go to the native iOS mapper instead, which usually shows "not
found" in a MAUI project). MAUI
matches in this order: the element's own identifier (AutomationId), its literal
text in XAML or code-behind, then a string resource (.resx). Native Android
matches: the element's own identifier (resource-id, or a Compose testTag only when
the app sets testTagsAsResourceId -- never trusted for an Android framework id
(package "android"), or for an id from a genuinely different app,
checked against the actual scanned app's own package first), its literal text in
layout XML or Kotlin/Java, then a strings.xml resource, then (Compose only) a
testTag template's longest matching fixed prefix (never "exact"). Native iOS matches: the element's
own accessibility identifier (or, rarely, one set from Interface Builder -- never
"exact"), its literal text in Swift/Objective-C/SwiftUI code
(NSLocalizedString and similar macros included), then a .strings/.xcstrings catalog
entry, then -- lower confidence, since it's often a decoy overwritten in code, and
never "exact" -- the
storyboard/XIB's own design-time text. React Native matches the element's own
testID (including a dynamic, per-row testID built from a fixed literal prefix),
then its literal accessibilityLabel/JSX text, then a translation key found in any
.json file under the source folder. Flutter matches Semantics(identifier: ...),
then a literal Text('...'), Semantics(label: ...) or Tooltip(message: ...), then a
.arb translation key. A translation-key match (React Native/Flutter) is always
"likely", never "exact". On any framework, an ambiguous match (the same text found
in more than one place) is narrowed by which file shares the most of the screen's
other finding labels and shown as "likely" (a best guess at the file, never "exact"
-- picking a file this way is still a guess), or left as several candidates when
nothing stands out. An unlabeled element with no literal text (common in a list
bound to data) can only be pointed at by its size, an adjacent label (MAUI, native
Android and UIKit only), or (MAUI only) its position in a repeating template -- also
shown as "likely" (a best guess at the line, never the exact runtime text) -- a
SwiftUI, React Native or Flutter element with no name is always "not found" instead
-- and never turned into a proposed code
change (only an exact match ever is; the inline example fix at that line only shows
for MAUI today). See the user guide for what "exact/likely/candidates/not found"
each mean. Nothing under this path is ever uploaded or sent anywhere; only local
files are read

options.name: --result-bundle
options.description:
iOS: use the physical-device result-bundle capture path even on a Simulator.
Advanced/testing use only; scans work correctly without it

options.name: --screen-reader
options.description:
Real screen-reader evidence next to the predicted transcript in the report.
Android: drives TalkBack over the screen's focusable elements and reads back
exactly what it says. Works with both scan (once, for the screen shown) and
record (once per screen you scan while recording). Off by default -- costs
roughly 1-2 seconds per element (a 30-element screen ~1 minute); entirely
local, on-device (see
docs/limitations.md). Turns TalkBack on for the capture and temporarily makes
a small helper app Swipewalk installs TalkBack's default text-to-speech
engine, so it receives the exact spoken text -- TalkBack speaks nothing aloud
for the length of the capture; don't use this on a phone someone is relying
on TalkBack with right now. The accessibility settings this changes (which
service is enabled, touch exploration, the default text-to-speech engine) are
restored three ways (this method's own restore, a marker read back at the
next run, and a timer armed on the device itself that restores those settings
on its own if Swipewalk stops or is disconnected from the phone). Once a
capture's restore is known to have succeeded, the helper app itself is
uninstalled too, taking its device permission with it; only left when a
restore failed or is pending, for the safety timer and doctor's own repair.
Tested with the device's
system language set to English, Spanish, Hindi, Arabic and Japanese;
TalkBack's own role and hint words follow that language, the app's own
wording does not. Needs TalkBack (Android Accessibility Suite) installed on
the device. On a physical phone, asks for confirmation first
(--screen-reader-confirm skips the prompt for a non-interactive run); use a
test device.
iOS (scan and record): walks Xcode's Accessibility Inspector on this Mac over
the macOS Accessibility API; VoiceOver itself is never turned on. Takes extra
time per element (a large screen can take a minute or more). Interactive only:
asks to use the macOS Accessibility permission for whichever app is running
Swipewalk (normally your terminal) -- which lets that app operate other apps
on this Mac; used here only for the Inspector, revocable any time in System
Settings -- then for a one-time manual step this can't do itself: opening
Accessibility Inspector, choosing the target device in its toolbar, and
clicking the first element (e.g. its title) on the app's screen. In record,
this is asked once per recording session (continuing a recording later asks
again), not once per screen. Declining, or a non-interactive run, falls back
to the predicted transcript; the report records why

options.name: --screen-reader-confirm
options.description:
Skip --screen-reader's Android physical-device confirmation prompt (required
instead of the prompt for a non-interactive run on a physical phone)

options.name: --web-audit
options.description:
Android only: also run axe-core (Deque's engine, bundled --
nothing to install) directly inside this screen's WebView content, over the
Chrome DevTools Protocol, for a deeper audit than the native accessibility tree
alone gives (for example the document's own <title>, and an unlabelled image
Android's own name fallback can hide -- see docs/limitations.md). Off by
default. Needs the app under test to be a debug build (or otherwise built with
WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true)); skipped, with a reason, when it
isn't, or when the screen has no WebView. Findings are marked for review, like
Google's Accessibility Test Framework's; duplicates of Swipewalk's own findings
are merged. Entirely local: axe-core runs inside the WebView on the device
itself, nothing is uploaded

options.name: --voiceover-captions
options.description:
iOS, record only, physical iPhone only (--device <udid> required; VoiceOver
does not run in the Simulator): tried on a real device on one screen only, in
English so far (see docs/limitations.md).
Per screen you scan while recording, offers to capture a person-driven VoiceOver
session -- you turn on VoiceOver and its Caption Panel (Settings > Accessibility
> VoiceOver > Caption Panel) yourself and swipe through the screen; Swipewalk
never turns VoiceOver on or scripts it. It polls screenshots of the phone over
the cable (no automation, no extra permission) and reads the on-screen caption
text with on-device text recognition, so the caption text Swipewalk managed to
read appears in the report next to the predicted transcript -- it can miss or
misread a caption, so treat it as a first look, not settled fact. Interactive
only; declining, or a non-interactive run, falls back to the predicted transcript

options.name: --large-text
options.description:
scan: also capture at a large system text size (Android 200%; iOS AX3, about 235%,
set through the Settings app on a physical iPhone). On a physical device this
changes the phone's text size and restores it; use a test device. record does
this by default

options.name: --appearance
options.description:
scan: also capture the screen in the device's other dark/light appearance (Android
`cmd uimode night`; iOS Simulator `simctl ui appearance`; a physical iPhone through
Settings > Appearance) and run every check on it too, so a contrast
failure that only shows up in one theme isn't missed just because the device
happened to be in the other one. Restores the device's original appearance
afterward, including on an error or Ctrl-C. Off by default. On a physical iPhone
left on Automatic, there's no fixed "current" appearance to switch from, so the
check is skipped there with a reason

options.name: --orientation
options.description:
scan: also rotate the device to its other orientation (portrait <-> landscape;
Android `settings put system accelerometer_rotation/user_rotation`; iOS via the
harness's XCUIDevice.shared.orientation, the same call for the Simulator and a
physical iPhone) and check whether the screen's content actually followed --
for review against WCAG 1.3.4 Orientation, since a single orientation can be
essential to a screen. When it does rotate, every check runs on that capture too.
Restores the device's orientation afterward (exactly, on Android, along with its
rotation-lock state; on iOS, back to whichever of portrait/landscape the first
capture showed, since there's no way to read the original back), including on an
error or Ctrl-C. Off by default. On a physical iPhone, there's no API to read
Control Center's rotation lock state; a test on iOS 27.0 found the interface still
rotated with the lock on, but that isn't confirmed on every iOS version -- if a
screen looks restricted, check with the lock off before concluding it's real

options.name: --auto-update-content
options.description:
scan: take a few further captures of this screen, spaced unevenly with no input
(each gap deliberately longer than the last, to catch a cycle a fixed interval
could alias with), and report any gap where content changed on its own (a
carousel, ticker, timer or auto-advancing banner) -- for review against WCAG
2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide, since a control to pause/stop/hide it may exist
elsewhere on the screen, the content may not be shown alongside anything else
(which 2.2.2 doesn't cover), or the update may be essential to an activity.
Never touches the device, so it works on a physical phone too. Off by default:
each extra capture costs a wait plus a full capture, fast on Android, much
slower on iOS (a full XCUITest harness capture); the report states the real
time elapsed, not an assumed one

options.name: --auto-update-interval
options.description:
Seconds to wait before the FIRST extra capture for --auto-update-content, on top
of however long that capture itself takes; later gaps target about 1.6x the one
before (default 3)

options.name: --standard
options.description:
scan/record/export: show one law or standard only, everywhere in the report:
ada-title-ii, section-508, en-301-549, en-301-549-v4, uk-public-sector, or a US state
/ other-country id from `swipewalk standards` (docs/standards.md). Without it every
issue says how many of all the mapped laws and standards it is relevant to, with the
full list under it. With export, relevance is worked out again from each issue's WCAG
criteria, so no rescan is needed; an ACR export ignores it (it is per WCAG criterion)

options.name: --my-laws
options.description:
scan/record/export: laws and standards that matter to you, as comma-separated ids
(same ids as --standard). Each issue then lists them first ("Relevant to ADA Title II,
Texas and N more", plus any chosen law the issue is outside of) and the laws table starts with them; every other law is still
there, after them. Kept in the run so a later export uses the same choice; also
"myLaws" in swipewalk.json. --standard, when given, still means only that one

options.name: --include-system
options.description: apps: also list the system apps, not only the ones installed by a person or a store

options.name: --delete
options.description: history: delete one saved run (folder or id); a recording still in progress is refused

options.name: --expect
options.description: record: comma-separated screens you meant to cover; missing ones are listed

options.name: --auto
options.description:
record: also scan automatically when the screen changes (default: off -- only
"Enter"/"Scan this screen now" captures a screen, so a screen is only captured
when you ask for it)

options.name: --continue
options.description:
session: carry on a saved screen reader session (see: swipewalk history) -- run
folder or id. New screens are added to the same run; a screen you open again
replaces its earlier recording, and the report says the run was recorded across
several sessions, with each one's times. The app comes from the run; --package is
refused if it names a different app. A session that ended normally can be continued too.
record: resume a recording that ended early (see: swipewalk history) -- run
folder or id, including one interrupted because Swipewalk itself was closed or
crashed (the next `history` or `--continue` sees that the recording process is
gone and lists the run as ended early). Appends new screens to that same run; rescanning
a screen already in it replaces the earlier capture, so it isn't counted twice.
--platform and the package/bundle id come from the run itself unless you override
them; --out is ignored (it always writes back into the run's own folder). Not
offered for a run that finished normally (Finish was chosen), or one still being
recorded (here, or in another window) -- record a new one, or wait, instead.

options.name: --large-text-restart
options.description:
Once a screen shows that checking the larger size needs the app restarted (the
text didn't change while the app kept running, or, on some Android apps, the
screen changed on its own): ask before restarting (default when the console can
prompt), always restart without asking, or never (the report says why the screen
wasn't checked). scan asks once, for the one screen it's checking; if a different
screen comes back after restarting, scan's own output points at `record` instead
(record lets you navigate back). record asks the same question about later screens too,
each check costing two extra navigations (back once the size is enlarged, then to
wherever you scan next once it's restored); "l" during a recording changes this
live. Non-interactive runs (redirected input, or `swipewalk run` unless
swipewalk.json sets "largeTextRestart": "ask") default to never for record (so an
unattended recording never blocks) and always for scan (so CI keeps checking large
text the way it always has).

options.description:
Android: keystore to sign a .aab install with, instead of the standard Android
debug key. Needs --keystore-alias, and the SWIPEWALK_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD environment
variable (SWIPEWALK_KEY_PASSWORD too if the key's own password differs -- rare for
a PKCS12 keystore, the default format since Java 8u60, which doesn't reliably
support a key password different from the keystore's own) -- a keystore password
is never taken on the command line or put in swipewalk.json

options.name: --keystore-alias
options.description: Android: key alias inside --keystore; required together with it

options.name: --package
options.description: Android: app package; the pre-flight check confirms it is installed and in front

options.name: --skip-checks
options.description: Skip the pre-flight checks that run before scan and record

options.name: --team
options.description:
iOS physical devices (also session --platform ios): Apple developer team that signs the scanning harness (found
automatically when the keychain has just one; a given team is remembered for next
time by `scan` run from a terminal, not by `record`, `session`, `swipewalk run`,
or a run whose input is redirected (scripts, CI))

options.name: --harness
options.description:
iOS: path to a harness project, for Swipewalk's maintainers (the harness that ships with
Swipewalk is used by default)

options.name: --android-harness
options.description:
Android: path to a harness project folder, for Swipewalk's maintainers (the prebuilt
harness that ships with Swipewalk is used by default; a missing or unbuildable harness
only skips Google's Accessibility Test Framework checks, never the scan -- see the
report/results.json for why)

options.name: --screen
options.description: Name for the scanned screen in the report (default: "Screen 1")

options.name: --out
options.description: Output directory (default: ./swipewalk-report); runs are also saved to the history

options.name: --no-history
options.description: Don't save this run to the history (scan, record and run)

options.name: --history
options.description:
History folder to save to (scan, record and run; default: the user's Swipewalk/runs
folder). Given explicitly, runs re-scanned with --from are saved too
With --app: history folder to read from (default: the user's Swipewalk/runs folder)
Triage options (swipewalk triage):

options.name: --from
options.description: Re-scan a saved capture directory instead of a live device

options.name: --carry-triage
options.description:
scan/record: after the run is saved, carry the triage marks of the previous run of the same app
and platform into it, the same way the desktop app does after every scan or recording: a mark is
carried only when exactly one finding on a matching screen matches it, never when more
than one could, and each carried mark says which run it came from. Off by default, so
existing output stays the same. Not with --no-history, --from or --continue

options.name: --triage
options.description:
scan/record: seed this run with an existing triage file's marks (see
`swipewalk triage`) before capturing anything, so its report shows them from the
start -- for a project file a team commits alongside their app (e.g.
swipewalk-triage.json). Without this, each run has its own triage.json in its
folder (the default `swipewalk triage <run>` writes to), started empty. compare and
export also accept --triage to read marks from elsewhere instead of the run's own
triage.json
Read triage marks from this file instead of the run's own triage.json. Every
format carries them: the CSV gets TriageStatus/TriageReason/TriageBy/TriageDate
columns, a Markdown ticket gets its own "## Triage" section, the HTML report shows
the same "Triaged by your team" group the report page does, and acr excludes a
finding marked false positive from its counts (disclosed in the row's remark) and
notes a won't-fix/accepted-risk mark next to the finding it still counts
Read and write marks in this file instead of the run's own triage.json -- e.g. a
project file committed alongside your app and shared across many runs of the same
app, rather than one run's own folder
A mark is never written into results.json (it stays a separate file, next to it); the run's report.html is
re-rendered immediately so it reflects the change without a rescan. A finding never reads as "fixed" or
"passed" because it was triaged -- it is still reported, just marked with who decided what and why.
Diagnostic log: every command also writes a short log on this computer (macOS ~/Library/Logs/Swipewalk,
Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Swipewalk\Logs, Linux ~/.local/state/swipewalk/logs or $XDG_STATE_HOME/swipewalk/logs):
versions, what ran, pre-flight results and errors, not the text on the screens you scan, with serial numbers,
device names, team IDs, your user name and home folder removed by pattern. Files more than a week old are
deleted, and older files are removed to keep the folder near 10 MB (checked when Swipewalk starts and once a day).
Set SWIPEWALK_LOG=debug in the terminal to also record the tool commands Swipewalk runs (adb, xcrun, xcodebuild...), with their arguments, exit codes and times.
Set SWIPEWALK_LOG_DIR to a full path to keep the log in another folder.
Nothing is ever sent; `swipewalk diagnostics` makes the file to attach to a bug report.
scan checks the screen currently shown (bringing the app forward, or starting it, first if needed).
record watches while you use the app; nothing is captured until you scan a screen (Enter, or --auto to
scan every new screen automatically). q finishes and writes the report. Exits with 2 if the recording
ended early (an error or a cancellation), and the report says so; screens after that point were not
scanned -- `record --continue <run>` resumes it later, appending screens to the same run rather than
starting a new one; the report then says it was recorded across more than one session, with each one's
times. If Swipewalk itself is closed or crashes mid-recording, there's no exit code to report that by --
but `swipewalk history` and `record --continue` notice the process is gone the next time you run them,
and list it as ended early, so it can be continued. run does what swipewalk.json describes and
exits with 3 when failOn is "wcag-issues" and issues were found. Output: results.json and report.html.
Automated checks find only some issues; manual testing is still required.

options.name: --framework
options.description:
App framework for fix examples and the report header: maui, androidviews,
jetpackcompose, uikit, swiftui, flutter, reactnative or hybridweb. Detected
automatically when possible (Android: from its own class names; iOS: MAUI on the
Simulator or an iPhone installed with --install, a WebView filling the screen on
either platform; iOS never detects UIKit/SwiftUI, and detects Flutter/React
Native only from the app bundle) -- pass this to override detection, or to name
the framework yourself when it can't be detected (see docs/limitations.md
"framework-detection-partial")

options.name: --source
options.description:
scan/record/export: path to the app's own project folder, read locally to point
each finding at a likely source line (e.g. "Source (exact match):
Views/LoginPage.xaml:42" in the report and exported tickets; the label differs by
confidence, see the user guide). 0.4: .NET MAUI, native Android Views/Jetpack
Compose, native iOS (storyboards/XIBs, UIKit, SwiftUI), React Native and Flutter.
Which mapper runs is picked from each screen's own detected framework: MAUI (either
platform) uses the MAUI mapper; an Android screen detected as Views/Compose or not
detected at all uses the Android mapper; an iOS screen detected as UIKit/SwiftUI or
not detected at all uses the native iOS mapper; a React Native or Flutter screen,
on either platform, always uses its own mapper; a hybrid-web screen matches none of
them (a physical iPhone needs --install or --framework maui for MAUI detection, or
its findings go to the native iOS mapper instead, which usually shows "not
found" in a MAUI project). MAUI
matches in this order: the element's own identifier (AutomationId), its literal
text in XAML or code-behind, then a string resource (.resx). Native Android
matches: the element's own identifier (resource-id, or a Compose testTag only when
the app sets testTagsAsResourceId -- never trusted for an Android framework id
(package "android"), or for an id from a genuinely different app,
checked against the actual scanned app's own package first), its literal text in
layout XML or Kotlin/Java, then a strings.xml resource, then (Compose only) a
testTag template's longest matching fixed prefix (never "exact"). Native iOS matches: the element's
own accessibility identifier (or, rarely, one set from Interface Builder -- never
"exact"), its literal text in Swift/Objective-C/SwiftUI code
(NSLocalizedString and similar macros included), then a .strings/.xcstrings catalog
entry, then -- lower confidence, since it's often a decoy overwritten in code, and
never "exact" -- the
storyboard/XIB's own design-time text. React Native matches the element's own
testID (including a dynamic, per-row testID built from a fixed literal prefix),
then its literal accessibilityLabel/JSX text, then a translation key found in any
.json file under the source folder. Flutter matches Semantics(identifier: ...),
then a literal Text('...'), Semantics(label: ...) or Tooltip(message: ...), then a
.arb translation key. A translation-key match (React Native/Flutter) is always
"likely", never "exact". On any framework, an ambiguous match (the same text found
in more than one place) is narrowed by which file shares the most of the screen's
other finding labels and shown as "likely" (a best guess at the file, never "exact"
-- picking a file this way is still a guess), or left as several candidates when
nothing stands out. An unlabeled element with no literal text (common in a list
bound to data) can only be pointed at by its size, an adjacent label (MAUI, native
Android and UIKit only), or (MAUI only) its position in a repeating template -- also
shown as "likely" (a best guess at the line, never the exact runtime text) -- a
SwiftUI, React Native or Flutter element with no name is always "not found" instead
-- and never turned into a proposed code
change (only an exact match ever is; the inline example fix at that line only shows
for MAUI today). See the user guide for what "exact/likely/candidates/not found"
each mean. Nothing under this path is ever uploaded or sent anywhere; only local
files are read
Path to the app's own project folder (.NET MAUI, native Android, native iOS,
React Native or Flutter), read locally to add a likely source line to findings
that don't already have one from the scan (see --source under Scan options
above). Useful when a run was scanned without the source available and the
source has since been found -- this only affects what's exported now, it never
rewrites the run's own results.json; not supported with --app

options.name: --result-bundle
options.description:
iOS: use the physical-device result-bundle capture path even on a Simulator.
Advanced/testing use only; scans work correctly without it

options.name: --screen-reader
options.description:
Real screen-reader evidence next to the predicted transcript in the report.
Android: drives TalkBack over the screen's focusable elements and reads back
exactly what it says. Works with both scan (once, for the screen shown) and
record (once per screen you scan while recording). Off by default -- costs
roughly 1-2 seconds per element (a 30-element screen ~1 minute); entirely
local, on-device (see
docs/limitations.md). Turns TalkBack on for the capture and temporarily makes
a small helper app Swipewalk installs TalkBack's default text-to-speech
engine, so it receives the exact spoken text -- TalkBack speaks nothing aloud
for the length of the capture; don't use this on a phone someone is relying
on TalkBack with right now. The accessibility settings this changes (which
service is enabled, touch exploration, the default text-to-speech engine) are
restored three ways (this method's own restore, a marker read back at the
next run, and a timer armed on the device itself that restores those settings
on its own if Swipewalk stops or is disconnected from the phone). Once a
capture's restore is known to have succeeded, the helper app itself is
uninstalled too, taking its device permission with it; only left when a
restore failed or is pending, for the safety timer and doctor's own repair.
Tested with the device's
system language set to English, Spanish, Hindi, Arabic and Japanese;
TalkBack's own role and hint words follow that language, the app's own
wording does not. Needs TalkBack (Android Accessibility Suite) installed on
the device. On a physical phone, asks for confirmation first
(--screen-reader-confirm skips the prompt for a non-interactive run); use a
test device.
iOS (scan and record): walks Xcode's Accessibility Inspector on this Mac over
the macOS Accessibility API; VoiceOver itself is never turned on. Takes extra
time per element (a large screen can take a minute or more). Interactive only:
asks to use the macOS Accessibility permission for whichever app is running
Swipewalk (normally your terminal) -- which lets that app operate other apps
on this Mac; used here only for the Inspector, revocable any time in System
Settings -- then for a one-time manual step this can't do itself: opening
Accessibility Inspector, choosing the target device in its toolbar, and
clicking the first element (e.g. its title) on the app's screen. In record,
this is asked once per recording session (continuing a recording later asks
again), not once per screen. Declining, or a non-interactive run, falls back
to the predicted transcript; the report records why

options.name: --screen-reader-confirm
options.description:
Skip --screen-reader's Android physical-device confirmation prompt (required
instead of the prompt for a non-interactive run on a physical phone)

options.name: --web-audit
options.description:
Android only: also run axe-core (Deque's engine, bundled --
nothing to install) directly inside this screen's WebView content, over the
Chrome DevTools Protocol, for a deeper audit than the native accessibility tree
alone gives (for example the document's own <title>, and an unlabelled image
Android's own name fallback can hide -- see docs/limitations.md). Off by
default. Needs the app under test to be a debug build (or otherwise built with
WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true)); skipped, with a reason, when it
isn't, or when the screen has no WebView. Findings are marked for review, like
Google's Accessibility Test Framework's; duplicates of Swipewalk's own findings
are merged. Entirely local: axe-core runs inside the WebView on the device
itself, nothing is uploaded

options.name: --voiceover-captions
options.description:
iOS, record only, physical iPhone only (--device <udid> required; VoiceOver
does not run in the Simulator): tried on a real device on one screen only, in
English so far (see docs/limitations.md).
Per screen you scan while recording, offers to capture a person-driven VoiceOver
session -- you turn on VoiceOver and its Caption Panel (Settings > Accessibility
> VoiceOver > Caption Panel) yourself and swipe through the screen; Swipewalk
never turns VoiceOver on or scripts it. It polls screenshots of the phone over
the cable (no automation, no extra permission) and reads the on-screen caption
text with on-device text recognition, so the caption text Swipewalk managed to
read appears in the report next to the predicted transcript -- it can miss or
misread a caption, so treat it as a first look, not settled fact. Interactive
only; declining, or a non-interactive run, falls back to the predicted transcript

options.name: --large-text
options.description:
scan: also capture at a large system text size (Android 200%; iOS AX3, about 235%,
set through the Settings app on a physical iPhone). On a physical device this
changes the phone's text size and restores it; use a test device. record does
this by default

options.name: --appearance
options.description:
scan: also capture the screen in the device's other dark/light appearance (Android
`cmd uimode night`; iOS Simulator `simctl ui appearance`; a physical iPhone through
Settings > Appearance) and run every check on it too, so a contrast
failure that only shows up in one theme isn't missed just because the device
happened to be in the other one. Restores the device's original appearance
afterward, including on an error or Ctrl-C. Off by default. On a physical iPhone
left on Automatic, there's no fixed "current" appearance to switch from, so the
check is skipped there with a reason

options.name: --orientation
options.description:
scan: also rotate the device to its other orientation (portrait <-> landscape;
Android `settings put system accelerometer_rotation/user_rotation`; iOS via the
harness's XCUIDevice.shared.orientation, the same call for the Simulator and a
physical iPhone) and check whether the screen's content actually followed --
for review against WCAG 1.3.4 Orientation, since a single orientation can be
essential to a screen. When it does rotate, every check runs on that capture too.
Restores the device's orientation afterward (exactly, on Android, along with its
rotation-lock state; on iOS, back to whichever of portrait/landscape the first
capture showed, since there's no way to read the original back), including on an
error or Ctrl-C. Off by default. On a physical iPhone, there's no API to read
Control Center's rotation lock state; a test on iOS 27.0 found the interface still
rotated with the lock on, but that isn't confirmed on every iOS version -- if a
screen looks restricted, check with the lock off before concluding it's real

options.name: --auto-update-content
options.description:
scan: take a few further captures of this screen, spaced unevenly with no input
(each gap deliberately longer than the last, to catch a cycle a fixed interval
could alias with), and report any gap where content changed on its own (a
carousel, ticker, timer or auto-advancing banner) -- for review against WCAG
2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide, since a control to pause/stop/hide it may exist
elsewhere on the screen, the content may not be shown alongside anything else
(which 2.2.2 doesn't cover), or the update may be essential to an activity.
Never touches the device, so it works on a physical phone too. Off by default:
each extra capture costs a wait plus a full capture, fast on Android, much
slower on iOS (a full XCUITest harness capture); the report states the real
time elapsed, not an assumed one

options.name: --auto-update-interval
options.description:
Seconds to wait before the FIRST extra capture for --auto-update-content, on top
of however long that capture itself takes; later gaps target about 1.6x the one
before (default 3)

options.name: --standard
options.description:
scan/record/export: show one law or standard only, everywhere in the report:
ada-title-ii, section-508, en-301-549, en-301-549-v4, uk-public-sector, or a US state
/ other-country id from `swipewalk standards` (docs/standards.md). Without it every
issue says how many of all the mapped laws and standards it is relevant to, with the
full list under it. With export, relevance is worked out again from each issue's WCAG
criteria, so no rescan is needed; an ACR export ignores it (it is per WCAG criterion)

options.name: --my-laws
options.description:
scan/record/export: laws and standards that matter to you, as comma-separated ids
(same ids as --standard). Each issue then lists them first ("Relevant to ADA Title II,
Texas and N more", plus any chosen law the issue is outside of) and the laws table starts with them; every other law is still
there, after them. Kept in the run so a later export uses the same choice; also
"myLaws" in swipewalk.json. --standard, when given, still means only that one

options.name: --include-system
options.description: apps: also list the system apps, not only the ones installed by a person or a store

options.name: --delete
options.description: history: delete one saved run (folder or id); a recording still in progress is refused

options.name: --expect
options.description: record: comma-separated screens you meant to cover; missing ones are listed

options.name: --auto
options.description:
record: also scan automatically when the screen changes (default: off -- only
"Enter"/"Scan this screen now" captures a screen, so a screen is only captured
when you ask for it)

options.name: --continue
options.description:
session: carry on a saved screen reader session (see: swipewalk history) -- run
folder or id. New screens are added to the same run; a screen you open again
replaces its earlier recording, and the report says the run was recorded across
several sessions, with each one's times. The app comes from the run; --package is
refused if it names a different app. A session that ended normally can be continued too.
record: resume a recording that ended early (see: swipewalk history) -- run
folder or id, including one interrupted because Swipewalk itself was closed or
crashed (the next `history` or `--continue` sees that the recording process is
gone and lists the run as ended early). Appends new screens to that same run; rescanning
a screen already in it replaces the earlier capture, so it isn't counted twice.
--platform and the package/bundle id come from the run itself unless you override
them; --out is ignored (it always writes back into the run's own folder). Not
offered for a run that finished normally (Finish was chosen), or one still being
recorded (here, or in another window) -- record a new one, or wait, instead.

options.name: --large-text-restart
options.description:
Once a screen shows that checking the larger size needs the app restarted (the
text didn't change while the app kept running, or, on some Android apps, the
screen changed on its own): ask before restarting (default when the console can
prompt), always restart without asking, or never (the report says why the screen
wasn't checked). scan asks once, for the one screen it's checking; if a different
screen comes back after restarting, scan's own output points at `record` instead
(record lets you navigate back). record asks the same question about later screens too,
each check costing two extra navigations (back once the size is enlarged, then to
wherever you scan next once it's restored); "l" during a recording changes this
live. Non-interactive runs (redirected input, or `swipewalk run` unless
swipewalk.json sets "largeTextRestart": "ask") default to never for record (so an
unattended recording never blocks) and always for scan (so CI keeps checking large
text the way it always has).

options.name: --format
options.description:
What to export a saved run's findings as: md writes one self-contained
Markdown ticket per finding (pasteable into Jira, GitHub Issues or Azure DevOps),
plus an images/ folder of evidence screenshots alongside them; csv writes one row
per finding for bulk import into Jira, Azure Boards or GitHub (never includes
screenshots -- an importer has nowhere to put them); html writes the whole report
as one self-contained file (screenshots embedded, shareable by email); pdf writes
the whole report as a tagged PDF (targeting PDF/UA-1, checked with veraPDF when
first added -- see docs/accessibility-statement.md for what's changed since;
needs nothing installed); acr writes a draft Accessibility Conformance Report -- for a
buyer evaluating the app, unlike the other formats which are for developers -- as
an OpenACR YAML file (openacr.yaml, github.com/GSA/openacr) plus a readable HTML
draft (acr-draft.html), both written into a
folder (default ./swipewalk-acr). It is a draft for you to
review and complete; whoever publishes the report is responsible for its
statements. One row per WCAG 2.2 Level A/AA success
criterion; a level is only ever "Supports" from a recorded manual pass with
evidence (this release doesn't record manual results, so no row reads that yet) --
a confirmed automated WCAG issue gives "Partially Supports", and "Not Evaluated"
covers everything else automated checks didn't confirm, including where they ran
and found nothing. Never "compliant", "certified" or "passes"; see the user guide
for exactly how each level is decided

options.name: --finding
options.description:
Export only this finding (repeat for several; md/csv only -- html, pdf and acr
always write the whole report; not supported at all with --app, which always
writes the whole combined report). Ids are in each exported ticket's Provenance
section and the CSV's FindingId column; a given id that doesn't match anything
prints the ids actually in this run. Without --finding, every finding in the run
is exported
The finding to mark (with --status/--reason) or unmark (with --clear). With no
--finding at all, lists every finding this run currently has a mark for, plus any
mark that no longer matches a finding in this run ("stale")

options.name: --no-screenshots
options.description:
Leave screenshots out of the export (md: no images/ folder; html/pdf: nothing
embedded; csv and acr are unaffected, neither includes them). No privacy warning
here: a test device is assumed, the same as everywhere else Swipewalk captures a
screenshot

options.name: --app-name
options.description:
acr only: product name for the report (default: the scanned app's package/bundle
id, or "Scanned app" if that's not known either)

options.name: --author-email
options.description:
acr only: contact email for the report's required "author" field (default: an
obvious placeholder, noted in the draft as needing to be filled in before sharing
it -- never auto-filled from your local identity)

options.name: --author-name
options.description: acr only: contact name alongside --author-email (optional in the OpenACR format)

options.name: --app
options.description:
Instead of <run>: combine specific saved runs of this app id (Android package,
iOS bundle id) into one report, across the run history rather than one run.
Requires --app-version and --run; see: swipewalk history for the ids and versions
recorded. This report covers only the screens in the scans you give it --
Swipewalk can't tell which screens your app has, so make sure they cover what you
need

options.name: --app-version
options.description:
With --app: which recorded app version to combine runs of (exactly as shown by
swipewalk history; "version not recorded" selects runs with no recorded version).
You choose the version -- nothing is decided for you
The app version this decision was made against; optional, purely informational

options.name: --run
options.description:
With --app/--app-version: combine this run (repeat for several). Required --
nothing is included by default; without it, this lists the version's saved runs
with a one-line summary of each so you can choose. An id that isn't actually a
run of the given app/version is reported and skipped, never silently guessed at

options.name: --use
options.description:
With --app: if the given --run runs captured the SAME screen more than once,
says which run's capture to use for it (repeat for several such screens). Without
it, on an interactive terminal you're asked; otherwise the run fails and lists
every screen that still needs a choice, with its options

options.name: --status
options.description:
What the team decided: false-positive (this isn't really an issue), wont-fix (a
real issue, not being fixed for now) or accepted-risk (a real issue the team is
knowingly leaving in place). For wont-fix and accepted-risk, everywhere the mark
is shown also states this never means the issue meets WCAG or any other standard.
Required together with --reason

options.name: --reason
options.description: Why (required together with --status; a triage mark is refused without one)

options.name: --by
options.description: Who made this decision, as free text (a name, a username, an email); optional

options.name: --clear
options.description:
Remove the current mark from --finding (its history is kept, not deleted -- see
the report's "stale" note if nothing else names this finding any more)

commands.name: checks
commands.description: Print every automated check as Markdown

commands.name: compare
commands.description: What changed between two runs (run folders

commands.name: diagnostics
commands.description: Save a diagnostic report for a bug report: one

options.name: --triage
options.description:
Read triage marks from this file instead of the run's own triage.json. Every
format carries them: the CSV gets TriageStatus/TriageReason/TriageBy/TriageDate
columns, a Markdown ticket gets its own "## Triage" section, the HTML report shows
the same "Triaged by your team" group the report page does, and acr excludes a
finding marked false positive from its counts (disclosed in the row's remark) and
notes a won't-fix/accepted-risk mark next to the finding it still counts
Read and write marks in this file instead of the run's own triage.json -- e.g. a
project file committed alongside your app and shared across many runs of the same
app, rather than one run's own folder
A mark is never written into results.json (it stays a separate file, next to it); the run's report.html is
re-rendered immediately so it reflects the change without a rescan. A finding never reads as "fixed" or
"passed" because it was triaged -- it is still reported, just marked with who decided what and why.
Diagnostic log: every command also writes a short log on this computer (macOS ~/Library/Logs/Swipewalk,
Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Swipewalk\Logs, Linux ~/.local/state/swipewalk/logs or $XDG_STATE_HOME/swipewalk/logs):
versions, what ran, pre-flight results and errors, not the text on the screens you scan, with serial numbers,
device names, team IDs, your user name and home folder removed by pattern. Files more than a week old are
deleted, and older files are removed to keep the folder near 10 MB (checked when Swipewalk starts and once a day).
Set SWIPEWALK_LOG=debug in the terminal to also record the tool commands Swipewalk runs (adb, xcrun, xcodebuild...), with their arguments, exit codes and times.
Set SWIPEWALK_LOG_DIR to a full path to keep the log in another folder.
Nothing is ever sent; `swipewalk diagnostics` makes the file to attach to a bug report.
scan checks the screen currently shown (bringing the app forward, or starting it, first if needed).
record watches while you use the app; nothing is captured until you scan a screen (Enter, or --auto to
scan every new screen automatically). q finishes and writes the report. Exits with 2 if the recording
ended early (an error or a cancellation), and the report says so; screens after that point were not
scanned -- `record --continue <run>` resumes it later, appending screens to the same run rather than
starting a new one; the report then says it was recorded across more than one session, with each one's
times. If Swipewalk itself is closed or crashes mid-recording, there's no exit code to report that by --
but `swipewalk history` and `record --continue` notice the process is gone the next time you run them,
and list it as ended early, so it can be continued. run does what swipewalk.json describes and
exits with 3 when failOn is "wcag-issues" and issues were found. Output: results.json and report.html.
Automated checks find only some issues; manual testing is still required.

options.name: --source
options.description:
Path to the app's own project folder (.NET MAUI, native Android, native iOS,
React Native or Flutter), read locally to add a likely source line to findings
that don't already have one from the scan (see --source under Scan options
above). Useful when a run was scanned without the source available and the
source has since been found -- this only affects what's exported now, it never
rewrites the run's own results.json; not supported with --app

options.name: --app-name
options.description:
acr only: product name for the report (default: the scanned app's package/bundle
id, or "Scanned app" if that's not known either)

options.name: --author-email
options.description:
acr only: contact email for the report's required "author" field (default: an
obvious placeholder, noted in the draft as needing to be filled in before sharing
it -- never auto-filled from your local identity)

options.name: --author-name
options.description: acr only: contact name alongside --author-email (optional in the OpenACR format)

options.name: --app
options.description:
Instead of <run>: combine specific saved runs of this app id (Android package,
iOS bundle id) into one report, across the run history rather than one run.
Requires --app-version and --run; see: swipewalk history for the ids and versions
recorded. This report covers only the screens in the scans you give it --
Swipewalk can't tell which screens your app has, so make sure they cover what you
need

options.name: --app-version
options.description:
With --app: which recorded app version to combine runs of (exactly as shown by
swipewalk history; "version not recorded" selects runs with no recorded version).
You choose the version -- nothing is decided for you
The app version this decision was made against; optional, purely informational

options.name: --run
options.description:
With --app/--app-version: combine this run (repeat for several). Required --
nothing is included by default; without it, this lists the version's saved runs
with a one-line summary of each so you can choose. An id that isn't actually a
run of the given app/version is reported and skipped, never silently guessed at

options.name: --use
options.description:
With --app: if the given --run runs captured the SAME screen more than once,
says which run's capture to use for it (repeat for several such screens). Without
it, on an interactive terminal you're asked; otherwise the run fails and lists
every screen that still needs a choice, with its options

options.name: --history
options.description:
With --app: history folder to read from (default: the user's Swipewalk/runs folder)
Triage options (swipewalk triage):

options.name: --status
options.description:
What the team decided: false-positive (this isn't really an issue), wont-fix (a
real issue, not being fixed for now) or accepted-risk (a real issue the team is
knowingly leaving in place). For wont-fix and accepted-risk, everywhere the mark
is shown also states this never means the issue meets WCAG or any other standard.
Required together with --reason

options.name: --reason
options.description: Why (required together with --status; a triage mark is refused without one)

options.name: --by
options.description: Who made this decision, as free text (a name, a username, an email); optional

options.name: --clear
options.description:
Remove the current mark from --finding (its history is kept, not deleted -- see
the report's "stale" note if nothing else names this finding any more)
